concept.name: Hybrid market
concept.definition: A market structure combining elements of auction/order-driven trading and dealer/quote-driven trading — typically an electronic limit order book operating alongside designated market makers or a floor auction with assigned liquidity obligations.
concept.intuition: Part robot, part human: most orders match electronically, but assigned market makers still quote and can step in when the book is thin.
concept.mechanics: A central order book provides automated execution, while registered market makers quote within it (and may receive obligations and privileges); some venues also retain a floor or single-price auction for the open, close, and volatile periods. The NYSE Hybrid Market, approved by the SEC in 2006, increased automated executions alongside its floor auction.
concept.failure_modes: The two mechanisms can conflict in stress: market maker obligations may be suspended exactly when needed, and interaction between automated quotes and human crowd interest can produce confusing or dual liquidity pools.
concept.misconceptions: Hybrid does not mean half-manual in a nostalgic sense — modern hybrids are overwhelmingly electronic, with human or obligated elements layered on top for specific functions like the opening auction.
concept.example: NYSE combines an electronic limit order book with Designated Market Makers who have quoting obligations and who facilitate the opening and closing auctions on the floor.

citations.source: SEC, Concept Release on Equity Market Structure (Release No. 34-61358)
citations.section: Section I and n.6 (NYSE Hybrid Market, Release No. 53539)
